units: the writer answers a close person who was worried about how she was doing
a move to a new home came before a stretch of broken sleep
the ringing of the phone made her body clench
someone she knows suggested she write her fears down at the end of the day
she thought the advice was pointless before she followed it
the writing brought up a recurring fear of being left behind
a specialist tied that anxious bond to her early years
she now tells the people close to her instead of shutting herself away
text: You asked in your note whether I was doing any better, so let me start where it started. The week we moved, sleep came apart, and every time the phone rang my shoulders locked up. A woman I know told me to write down, each evening, whatever had tightened my throat that day. The advice struck me as pointless. I did it anyway. Ten evenings in, the same fear kept surfacing on the page: that the people I love would leave me behind. A psychologist told me this anxious kind of attachment takes shape early, in the first years, and that it eases once you dare to ask for help. So now I tell my friends when I am sinking, instead of vanishing without a word. It still costs me something, I will not pretend otherwise. Last night I laughed out loud without watching myself do it. Write soon, and tell me about your week.

units: a mental health specialist takes questions about thoughts that keep repeating
the brain meets a threat to a bond almost the way it meets a threat to the body
the scene is played again in the hope of finding a way out
the replay keeps the alarm on rather than settling it
the alarm in turn sets the repeating thoughts going again
sleep breaks up because the inner watch does not stop at night
the people nearby tire of the same complaint and pull back
that withdrawal deepens the loneliness of the one who broods
the specialist advises writing the whole episode out a single time
text: What becomes of a slight you cannot put down? We put the question to a clinical psychologist who studies thinking that will not stop repeating. Her answer starts with the brain, which meets a threat to a bond almost the way it meets a threat to the body, and so it runs the scene again, hoping this time to reach a way out. Does the replay help? Not at all. It keeps the alarm switched on, and the alarm sends the thoughts round once more. Why does sleep break up? Because the watchman inside never goes off duty at night. And the people nearby? They hear the same complaint until they are worn thin, and they pull back, which leaves the brooder more alone than before. Her advice is to write the episode out end to end, one single evening, then close the notebook. A thought put into sentences stops turning on itself.

units: a young girl admits she cannot put what she feels into words
her aunt does not push and pours her something hot to drink
the aunt says she kept quiet at the same age out of reserve
the aunt holds that such silence shuts a person in rather than shielding her
the girl is afraid her words will make her mother cry
the aunt suggests locating the sensation instead of naming the sorrow
the girl points to two places on her neck
her breathing loosens once she has described them
they agree on a flat hand on the table as an arranged signal
the mother sits down beside her and asks nothing
text: The girl said she could not put what she felt into words, and she said it to the carpet rather than to her aunt. Her aunt let it sit for a while and poured out something hot to drink, then admitted that at that age she had held her tongue as well, out of reserve. Silence, she said, shields nobody at all. It only shuts you in alone. Her niece answered that words felt too heavy, and that hers would make her mother cry. So the aunt offered a way round: do not name the sorrow, find where it lodges. The girl pointed to her throat, then to the back of her neck, and her breathing loosened once she had said it. They settled on a quiet sign. A flat hand on the table would mean it was time to talk. That evening the hand came down, and her mother sat beside her and asked nothing at all.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: with no instruments to hand, early practitioners went by what patients told them
their approach joined long listening to the matching of similar cases
later practitioners took readings from the body
those readings included the beat of the heart and the length of sleep
the early approach caught the fine grain but missed the regularities
the instrument based approach caught the regularities but lost the fine grain
a feeling pushed out of awareness yields no measurable sign
the two approaches were later brought together
each one covers what the other cannot see
text: Before recording instruments were available, physicians described disorders of mood from what patients told them and nothing else. They listened at length, then set one case beside another to see what held across both. Clinicians trained later worked from the body instead, taking readings of the heartbeat, of the sweat on the skin, of how long a night of sleep ran. The older way caught the fine grain and missed the regularity; the instrument based way found regularities and let the fine grain slip. The split follows from the object itself. A feeling pushed out of awareness leaves no reading behind, while a reaction of the body writes itself down. The two traditions were eventually braided together: the patient is questioned while his inner reactions are tracked, and the two records are then compared. Neither one replaces the other, and each covers what its neighbor cannot see.

units: three kinds of signs give away that someone is uncomfortable
the first sign lies in the posture, with the shoulders drawn in
a hand carried toward the face goes with that posture
the second sign lies in the voice, whose pace weakens
the third sign lies in the eyes, which settle nowhere
discomfort bears on the picture one presents to others
fear, by contrast, bears on a danger coming from outside
shame stands apart because it runs longer and cuts deeper
an observer who notices can soften his voice and look away
text: Three kinds of signs give away that the person across from you is uncomfortable. The first lies in the posture: the shoulders draw in, the chin drops, and a hand rises toward the face as though to cover it. The second lies in the voice, whose pace weakens, whose sentences break off, and which loses its footing. The third lies in the eyes, which slide away, come back in short touches, then settle nowhere. What separates these signals from those of fear is their target, since discomfort bears on the picture one presents to others, whereas fear answers to a danger coming from outside. They differ from shame as well, which runs longer and cuts deeper and drives a person to withdraw entirely. Reading them serves the observer above all: he can soften his voice, look away, leave a gap in the exchange. Such restraint often makes the conversation bearable for the one who feels exposed.

units: a singer who is not a professional auditions in a borrowed hall
he had rehearsed for several weeks
a wave of dizziness took him as soon as he reached the platform
his hands went cold and his voice missed the opening
the panel granted him a second try
that second attempt came out worse than the first
a musician suggested he stand with his back to the audience
the performance then came out true and easy
afterward he took the ending again facing the room
he puts his trouble down to being watched rather than to the singing
text: An amateur singer turned up for an audition in a hall lent out by a society of musicians. He had rehearsed the piece for weeks and believed he was ready. The moment he reached the platform, the room tilted under him. The ceiling seemed to come down, his hands went cold, and his voice missed the opening note. He asked to start over, and the panel let him. The second attempt came out worse than the first. One of the players at the keyboard then suggested he sing with his back to the room. He laughed, and then he tried it. The piece came out whole, true, very nearly easy. They asked him afterward to turn round and take the last verse again, and he sang it without a tremor. What had frightened him, he decided, was never the singing but the eyes on him, and a tiny detour had been enough to disarm it.

units: the first step is to spot the bodily signal of anxiety
putting a word on the feeling takes some of its force away
you have to write down precisely the outcome you dread
you then set the harm you imagine against how likely it really is
stretching the outbreath slows the beat of the heart
arriving early spares you the tension of a room already full
planting your feet on the floor tells the brain the body is steady
asking for a drink breaks the runaway if panic takes hold
text: Start by catching the moment your stomach knots up before a meeting, because a feeling with a word on it loses some of its force. Then put down in your notebook exactly what you dread: being cut off, coming across as useless, sitting through an awkward silence. Write the harm you picture, and beside it the odds that it happens. The gap will jump out at you. Breathe after that, stretching the air on the way out, since it is the outbreath and not the intake that slows the heart. Come early, because walking into a room already full winds you up, while taking your seat before the others lets the tension drop away. Through the meeting, keep both feet planted flat on the floor, since that contact tells the brain the body is steady. And if panic climbs anyway, ask for water. The gesture gives you something to hold and breaks the runaway.

units: a place offering psychological support opened on a street of shops
the men who came in flared up during the first session
those men did not turn up for the sessions that followed
the team first put these departures down to a lack of willingness
the front room could be seen from the street through a pane of glass
being exposed to onlookers turned discomfort into aggression
the entrance was moved round to the courtyard side
a curtain went up and the lighting was brought down
the number of people breaking off treatment fell by half
the director advises studying the place before explaining a behavior
text: In an old quarter, a house offering support opened at the end of a lane lined with shops. The staff kept meeting the same wall. Men who came in for help flared up during the first interview, and then never turned up again. The team put it down at first to a lack of willingness. Closer watching told another story: the front room was glazed toward the lane, which left visitors on show to anyone walking past, and their discomfort came out as anger. What worked was a change of building before it was a change of treatment. The entrance was moved round to the inner courtyard, a heavy curtain went up, the lighting was brought down. Within one season, the number of people breaking off after the first appointment had fallen by half. The director repeats the lesson to her trainees: before you read a behavior, study the place that produced it.

units: a waiting room stands apart from the other spaces in the building
its walls are a muted green against a very bright corridor
the seats in it are turned toward one another
in the corridor the seats are lined up along the wall
a thick floor covering smothers the sound of footsteps
the hard floor of the entrance, by contrast, throws the noise back
worn magazines lie on a low piece of furniture
those who arrive show a sharp restlessness in voice and gesture
they leave the room walking at a steadier pace
text: The waiting room at that practice is like no other space in the building. Its walls carry a muted green, while the corridor beside it snaps with white. In here the armchairs turn a little toward one another, as though they expected a conversation. Out there the chairs run flat along the wall. A thick rug swallows the sound of footsteps, whereas the hard floor of the entrance throws every heel back at you. On the low table lie tired magazines, scruffier than the ones at the front desk, and perhaps it is that untidiness that reassures. Those who come in are often keyed up, the voice pitched high, the hands quick. They go out again at a steadier pace, the jaw unclenched. The room cures nothing, of course. Like an airlock, it only prepares the crossing from one inner state to another.

units: the writer disputes the idea that sadness is a fault to be put right
an emotion reports what holds value for the person feeling it
the pace of digital exchange makes a lasting mood look suspect
that pressure leads people to dread their own inner slowness
methods of assessment favor whatever can be counted
inner experience therefore escapes the studies, since it cannot be coded
a feeling pushed down comes back as irritability or exhaustion
the writer grants that pain which drags on calls for treatment
treating ordinary sorrow as an illness robs people of the words to speak of themselves
text: We ought to stop handling sadness as a breakdown in need of repair. First point: an emotion is no fault in the manufacture, but a report on what holds value for the person feeling it. Second point: the pace our screens demand casts suspicion on any mood that lasts, so that people end up dreading their own inner slowness. Third point: protocols of assessment favor whatever can be counted, and inner experience, hard to code, drops out of the studies altogether. Fourth point: a feeling pushed down does not fade away, it comes back elsewhere, as irritability or as a tiredness that will not lift. Someone will object that pain which drags on calls for treatment, and the objection is sound. But to fold ordinary sorrow into illness is to rob everyone of the words for saying what they are living through.
